title: fetch & HTTP client
lede: The WHATWG fetch client — fetch(), Response, Request, Headers — over libcurl, non-blocking under the event loop. The response body accessors (.text()/.json()/.arrayBuffer()) return a real Promise<T> you await — a genuine thenable, so .then() and Promise.all() work on them. The body accessors settle off the transfer's completion (ADR-00823), so a .json() parse error is a promise rejection and the download overlaps intervening work. WebSocket, EventSource, and XMLHttpRequest are separate Networking surfaces, documented elsewhere.

entries.name: fetch(url, init?)
entries.signature: fetch(url: string | Request, init?: RequestInit): Promise<Response>
entries.description: Issues an HTTP request and resolves when the response headers arrive; the body is read lazily. Genuinely non-blocking — awaited inside an http.listen handler it yields to the event loop, so a slow upstream call doesn't stall other connections. A network-level failure (DNS, connection refused, TLS, timeout) throws; a non-2xx HTTP status still resolves normally — .ok distinguishes it, matching real fetch.

params.name: url
params.desc: The target URL, or a Request object as the sole argument.

params.name: init?
params.desc: A RequestInit: method, headers (any HeadersInit) and body (any BodyInit — a string, URLSearchParams, Blob, ArrayBuffer or TypedArray/Buffer, sent with the Content-Type undici implies), signal.

entries.snippet:
const r = await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8765/get')
console.log(r.status, r.ok)   // 200 true
differences: A network failure rejects with a TypeError whose message is libcurl's ("Couldn't connect to server"); Node's is "fetch failed", with the reason as its cause.

entries.name: Response.status / .ok
entries.signature: readonly status: number; readonly ok: boolean
entries.description: The HTTP status code, and whether it is in the 2xx range. A non-2xx response still resolves — check .ok rather than relying on fetch to throw.
entries.snippet:
const missing = await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8765/status/404')
console.log(missing.status, missing.ok)   // 404 false

entries.name: Response.text()
entries.description: Reads the body to completion and resolves to it as a string. Returns a real Promise<string> — await it, or chain .then().

returns.desc: Resolves to the response body as text.

entries.snippet:
const r = await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8765/get')
const body: string = await r.text()
differences: The result is a null-terminated string: a binary body with an embedded null byte truncates at the first one — use `.arrayBuffer()` for binary.

entries.name: Response.json()
entries.description: Reads and parses the body as JSON, resolving to a value projected into a declared type. Returns a real Promise<T> — await it, or chain .then(). Reuses JSON.parse's machinery — validates the body (a non-JSON body throws a catchable SyntaxError) and projects nested objects, array/object-array fields, and top-level T[].

returns.desc: Resolves to the parsed value, projected to the annotated type.

entries.snippet:
interface Ip { origin: string }
const info: Ip = await (await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8765/ip')).json()
differences: A JSON parse error rejects the promise (reachable via `.then`'s onRejected / `.catch`); the body settles off the transfer's completion (ADR-00823).
A typed declaration `const p: T = await r.json()` parses straight into `T` (the `JSON.parse`-style projection carve-out).
Only `any`/`unknown` dynamic shapes are unsupported; every statically-typed shape projects.
Same embedded-null truncation as `.text()` — the body is read as a null-terminated string.

entries.name: Response.arrayBuffer()
entries.description: Reads the body to completion and resolves to an ArrayBuffer, carrying the real byte count and coming back whole regardless of content. The binary-safe body accessor — use it for any body that may contain null bytes. Returns a real Promise<ArrayBuffer> — await it, or chain .then().

returns.desc: Resolves to the complete response body as bytes.

entries.snippet:
const binary = await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8765/bytes/16')
const bytes = new Uint8Array(await binary.arrayBuffer())

entries.name: Response.body
entries.signature: readonly body: ReadableStream<Uint8Array> | null; readonly bodyUsed: boolean
entries.description: A real ReadableStream<Uint8Array> fed incrementally from libcurl's write callback with backpressure via curl pause/unpause. Every read is the same stream; a constructed Response without a body has a null body. bodyUsed turns true once a body method runs or the stream is read, and a body method on a used or locked body rejects with a TypeError ("Body is unusable"), as in Node.

entries.name: new Response(body, init) / Response.json() / .redirect() / .error()
entries.statusRow: new Response(body, init) / Response.json() / Response.redirect() / Response.error()
entries.signature: new Response(body?: string | Uint8Array | ArrayBuffer | Blob | URLSearchParams | ReadableStream<Uint8Array> | null, init?: { status?: number, statusText?: string, headers?: HeadersInit }); Response.json(data, init?); Response.redirect(url, status?); Response.error()
entries.description: Builds a Response without a request: the body with the content type it implies (text/plain;charset=UTF-8 for a string, a Blob's own type) unless the headers set one, init's status, statusText and headers. Response.json serializes data as application/json, Response.redirect sets Location from the parsed URL, Response.error() is status 0 with type 'error'. text(), json(), arrayBuffer() and .body read it as they read a fetched Response; a ReadableStream body is .body itself, read to its end by a body method, and no body makes .body null.

returns.desc: A Response with the given body and init.

differences: A stream body must be a `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>`: a stream of `any` chunks is rejected at compile time.

entries.name: Response headers
entries.description: Reading response headers is not supported — no HEADERFUNCTION capture exists in this codebase yet. There is no .headers accessor on a Response, and XMLHttpRequest's .getResponseHeader()/.getAllResponseHeaders() are absent for the same reason. Request-side headers work fully.

entries.name: new Request(url, init?)
entries.signature: new Request(url: string, init?: RequestInit): Request
entries.description: A real Request class bundling a URL with method/headers/body: .url/.method/.headers, and Fetch's Body members (.body as a ReadableStream, bodyUsed, text()/json()/arrayBuffer()). method defaults to "GET" (standard methods case-normalized), headers to an empty Headers, body to null; a string body implies text/plain;charset=UTF-8, and a GET/HEAD request with a body is a TypeError. Works as fetch's sole argument, or supply a plain-object init to fetch directly.
differences: Its Headers keeps names lowercased, iterates in insertion order, and joins repeated set-cookie values.

entries.name: new Headers()
entries.description: A case-insensitive (lowercased-key) header bag. get/set/has/delete behave like Map<string,string>'s own — because storage-wise it is one. A real Headers instance is accepted anywhere fetch takes headers, alongside a plain Map<string,string>.

entries.name: Headers.append(name, value)
entries.description: Adds a header value, combining with a comma if name is already present instead of overwriting — the one behavior that distinguishes it from .set().
